title: Minor injuries reported after car v. snowplow crash in Oneida County - WSAW
content: SUGAR CAMP, Wis. (WSAW) - Only minor injuries were reported after a car and a snowplow crashed near Sugar Camp Monday morning. The crash was reported just after 8 a.m. near Cty Hwy A and King Rd. According to the Oneida County Sheriff’s Office, the car was split in half. The 17-year-old driver of the car reported minor injuries. The sheriff’s office says it appears the icy road conditions contributed to the crash. title: The Designated Director’s Dilemma: Lessons from Zync, Inc. v. Porsche Invs. Mgmt., S.A. - The National Law Review
content: The National Law Review uses cookies to track usage trends and patterns to better understand and improve our website. By using this website and/or clicking on any link on the website, you confirm your consent to the NLR’s placing and usage of cookies. The recent Delaware Court of Chancery decision in Zync, Inc. v. Porsche Invs. Mgmt., S.A., highlights the perils of the designated-director arrangement — a common feature in venture capital transactions where an investor secures a seat on a board of directors. Porsche Investments Management (“Porsche”) invested $2.9 million in Zync, Inc. (“Zync”), a cloud-based in-vehicle entertainment startup corporation. In return for the investment, Zync issued Porsche a convertible note (the “Porsche Note”) and 305,430 shares of common stock, representing 5 percent of the company’s equity on a fully diluted basis. The parties also entered into a voting rights agreement under which Zync committed to maintain a three-member board of directors (the “Board”) and granted Porsche the right to designate one director (the “Porsche Director”). Finally, the parties entered into an investor rights agreement under which Zync was prohibited from taking specified actions without the approval of the Porsche Director, which included an effective “veto” right relating to Zync’s ability to raise capital. Porsche designated its employee, Christian Knörle, to serve on the Board as the Porsche Director. After joining the Board, at the direction of Porsche, Knörle “vetoed” several financings that would have raised needed capital for Zync. Ultimately, Zync was forced to shut down. Zync sued Knörle for breach of fiduciary duty and bad faith conduct, and Porsche for aiding and abetting Knörle’s breaches of fiduciary duty, tortious interference with prospective economic advantage, and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing inherent in the investor rights agreement. Knörle and Porsche moved to dismiss the complaint for failure to state a claim on which relief can be granted. The Court denied the motion. This alert focuses on Knörle’s duties as the Porsche Director. In a follow-up alert, we will examine Porsche’s potential exposure for aiding and abetting Knörle’s alleged fiduciary breaches and focus on whether Zync expands the Court’s earlier decision in In re PLX Tech. Inc. S’holders Litig. Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster squarely addressed the “dual-fiduciary problem” that arises when a designated director owes competing loyalties. As Knörle owed fiduciary duties to Zync and its stockholders and to Porsche as his employer, a conflict of interest was reasonably conceivable1 whenever Porsche directed him to withhold consent for financings that were in Zync’s best interests. The Court found that Knörle inferably breached his fiduciary duty of loyalty and acted in bad faith by deferring to Porsche rather than exercising independent judgment. To counter the “dual-fiduciary problem,” Porsche contended that it could not conceivably have a conflict of interest with Zync because it backed Zync as a noteholder and owned shares of Zync as a stockholder. Relying on Katell v. Morgan Stanley Gp., Inc., Porsche invoked the general rule that it would have been irrational to harm Zync because that would impair the value of its common shares and reduce the likelihood of repayment on the Porsche Note. In rejecting Porsche’s argument, the Court noted: [T]here are exceptions to any general rule. Circumstances may cause the interests of a director and its affiliated investor to diverge from the interests of corporation and its stockholders as a whole. For example, “particular types of investors may espouse short-term investment strategies and structure their affairs to benefit economically from those strategies, thereby creating a divergent interest in pursuing short-term performance at the expense of long-term wealth.” A desire for liquidity may also cause an investor and its affiliated director to face a conflict. Zync, 2026 WL 1507812, at *9 (quoting In re PLX Tech. Inc. S’holders Litig., 2018 WL 5018535, at *41 (Del. Ch. Oct. 16, 2018)). Additionally, to counter Porsche’s argument, the Court recognized that Zync alleged that Porsche employs a “catch and kill” investment strategy: Porsche employs a “catch and kill” investment strategy that involves making a seed investment in a startup in return for governance rights, then using the governance rights to block other sources of capital. By making the startup dependent on Porsche, Porsche gains control of its new and potentially disruptive technology. If Porsche wants to deploy the technology, it can. If not, Porsche can force the startup to shut down, while maintaining control over its intellectual property. Finally, Knörle argued that he acted in good faith to pursue Zync’s best interests. As support, Knörle relied on his vote in favor of certain other forms of financing. The Court rejected this argument, noting that Knörle voted in favor of financing that he arguably did not have the power to veto. The Court also emphasized: Equity is not so blind. It regards the substance rather than the form. Directors can breach their duties through informal action and conscious inaction. Knörle breached his duty of loyalty by consciously preventing the Board from taking action. The core issue addressed in Zync involves the inherent conflict of interest that exists if an investor-designated director exercises “veto” rights on behalf of the director’s employer rather than acting in the interest of the corporation and its stockholders. Based on Zync, practitioners should take note that the designating investor’s instructions are not a “safe harbor” for the designated director under Delaware law. In fact, according to the Court, Delaware law demands undivided loyalty to the corporation and its stockholders, irrespective of whether the director was elected by the stockholders, appointed by the directors, or designated by an investor. title: Brentford v Everton - match preview, kick-off time and more - Brentford FC
content:
Analysis, team news, match officials and more. Here's everything you need to know ahead of Brentford's Premier League game against Everton at Gtech Community Stadium on Monday (8pm kick-off GMT, live on Sky Sports) Analysis, team news, match officials and more - here's everything you need to know ahead of the game. After the latest international hiatus, Brentford welcome David Moyes’ Everton to Gtech Community Stadium - where the Bees will have to contend with arguably the Premier League’s most in-form striker. Igor Thiago ran the Toffees ragged in both top-flight fixtures between the two clubs last season: the Brazilian netting a hat-trick in Brentford’s 4-2 win at Hill Dickinson Stadium at the start of the year followed by a brace in April’s 2-2 draw back in TW8. With Thiago suspended following his red card at Brighton, Brentford will be without their Brazilian striker this time round - but face an Everton striker in a purple patch. The rangy Thierno Barry reached double figures for the season with two strikes against Coventry before the break and the 24-year-old Frenchman has hit his stride after a slow-burning start to life on Merseyside, scoring four goals in his last three appearances for the Blues. Brentford may trail only Leeds United in the Premier League when it comes to successful aerial duels this season, but the Bees’ backline will need to gear up to face Barry - who has won more aerials (45) than any other player in the division over the first 10 matchweeks. With six top-flight goals to his name this season, the former Basel and Villarreal striker sits behind Erling Haaland (nine) and Alexander Isak (seven) in the Premier League scoring charts - but his underlying numbers highlight his knack for getting into dangerous goalscoring positions. Barry has accumulated more expected goals (9.53 xG) than any other player in the division - his xG per shot of 0.26 underlining the high quality of the chances coming his way. The Frenchman has also fired home four Carabao Cup goals to help Everton reach the quarter-finals, but hot on his heels in the competition’s scoring charts is Brentford’s Callum Wilson - who could lead the line for the Bees in Thiago’s absence. Signed on a free transfer from West Ham in the summer, Wilson struck in all three of the Bees’ Carabao Cup fixtures, demonstrating that his eye for goal remains undimmed. A sharp finish from outside the box in the 6-1 win over Birmingham City in round two showcased the 34-year-old’s ability to fashion a yard of space and pull the trigger from distance. A clinical strike at the end of a sweeping counter attack against Reading and a close-range effort versus Sunderland further demonstrated the variety in his finishing repertoire. One of the Premier League’s most prolific substitutes last season, Wilson will look to pounce if handed a first top-flight start for the Bees - and his set-piece smarts could prove particularly valuable. Last season, only Manchester United’s Casemiro (eight) and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk (six) scored more goals from free-kicks, corners and throw-ins than Wilson, who netted five of his seven Premier League goals for West Ham in 2025/26 from set-piece situations. Will Wilson make life sticky for the Toffees? Will Barry make it a Blue Monday for the Bees? We’ll find out under the Gtech lights. It looked as though Everton were in with a great chance of ending their near-decade-long exile from European football at the end of last season. They blew Chelsea away at Hill Dickinson Stadium on 21 March and moved into eighth, five points behind Aston Villa in fourth, with seven games left to play. Speaking to the BBC after that game, manager David Moyes said: "We're here now, I don't want to step away because you don't get many chances, so I think every game we have to see if we can get points and see if we can give ourselves a chance of getting into one of the European competitions." They subsequently buckled, however, falling behind in five of those seven and only clawing back three points, on the way to finishing 13th for the second season in a row. But the table was so congested that two more wins would have seen them finish in the top seven and return to Europe for the first time since 2017/18. Moyes admitted his frustration after the 1-0 defeat to Tottenham on the final day. "For three quarters of the season we've been very good; the last six or seven weeks we've been really disappointed," he said. "If we were coming here with two points more we'd come here with a different mindset." His frustration extended to Everton's summer recruitment. According to Sky Sports data, the Toffees were the fourth-lowest spenders in the division - and were left with just one out-and-out striker. “We don’t have a huge squad but sometimes you need to do something special in football and we will attempt to do something special,” Moyes said in September. To his credit, the beginnings of something special have been on show. Stoppage-time equalisers against Bournemouth and Manchester United helped them to go unbeaten in the first six. A difficult October, during which they collected just one point from a possible nine, has since given way to two consecutive league wins for the first time since March. They've kept four clean sheets in 10, have conceded the joint-fourth fewest goals in the Premier League (10) and have reached the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, where they will face League Two Fleetwood Town. And that one out-and-out striker? Thierno Barry - who scored eight goals last season - has 10 in 13 in all competitions already. “I want to make this season mine, so I just work a lot every time to do my best," he told evertontv after his double in the 3-1 win over Coventry in October. Moyes wants to get Everton back into Europe - it's the natural next step. And in Opta Analyst's current predicted table, they sit eighth. That would be the best finish since 2018/19 under Marco Silva - and potentially be enough to secure that spot the Scot craves. But that ambition may hinge on how much backing Moyes receives in January. Like the majority of his managerial colleagues in the Premier League, David Moyes had a long and successful playing career before turning his hand to coaching. He started at Celtic as a professional in 1980, where he won the Scottish league title in 1981/82, and went on to play for Cambridge United, Bristol City, Shrewsbury, Dunfermline Athletic, Hamilton and Preston. He was part of the North End squad that won the Third Division in 1995/96 and he retired at the age of 35, having played his last game in February 1998. By this point, he had been appointed Preston manager, a role for which he was well-equipped, having started taking his coaching badges in his early 20s. Just over four years later, in March 2002, he was approached by Everton and soon swapped the First Division for the Premiership. During his first spell on Merseyside, Moyes brought a 16-year-old Wayne Rooney into the first team and into the eyes of the world and, from 2006/07 to 2012/13, steered the Toffees to seven straight top-eight finishes, as well as reaching the 2008/09 FA Cup final, which they lost 2-1 to Chelsea. In the summer of 2013, he was given the unenviable task of replacing Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United, but lasted less than a year of the six-year deal he signed and was sacked in April 2014. A year in La Liga with Real Sociedad followed, where he won only 12 of his 42 games in charge, before he returned to England with Sunderland. It was just eight victories from 43 matches there, with his spell ending in the Black Cats’ relegation after a decade in the top flight. Moyes was handed a six-month deal to take over at West Ham in November 2017 and tasked with securing survival after the sacking of Slaven Bilić, which he did. However, his contract was not extended in the summer and he departed London Stadium after 31 games and a 29 per cent win ratio. The Scot returned to east London in December 2019 and was in charge of the Hammers until the end of the 2023/24 season, when his contract was not renewed. He oversaw the historic Europa Conference League win in 2022/23 and left with the highest win percentage of the club's permanent managers, with 44.59 across 231 games in his second spell. Moyes returned to management after a short spell away from the game, returning to Everton on a two-and-a-half-year contract on 11 January 2025. The 63-year-old has managed 764 Premier League games. Connor O'Neill, Everton correspondent for the Liverpool Echo, explains how David Moyes' side are likely to line up at the Gtech. "Everton will play their usual 4-2-3-1, which they have largely operated in this season," he told brentfordfc.com. "It will be a back four of Merlin Röhl or Jake O'Brien at right-back, Jarrad Branthwaite and James Tarkowski in the middle and Vitalii Mykolenko at left-back. "The midfield three will be James Garner, Harrison Armstrong and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, with Tyrique George on one side, possibly Röhl on the right if O'Brien plays at right-back, then Thierno Barry up front." Last Premier League starting XI v Coventry City (4-2-3-1): Pickford; Röhl, Tarkowski, Branthwaite, Mykolenko; Armstrong, Garner; Dibling, Dewsbury-Hall, George; Barry Aaron Hickey and Nathan Collins will miss Monday night's game against Everton after sustaining injuries on international duty. Hickey has suffered a hamstring injury and is expected to be sidelined for a number of weeks, while Collins has picked up a knee issue and will also be out for the next few weeks. There was more positive news on Fábio Carvalho, who has a chance of returning to the matchday squad against Everton. Josh Dasilva and Antoni Milambo are also continuing their respective recoveries and are due to feature for Brentford B on Sunday, while Rico Henry and Kaye Furo remain sidelined. Craig Pawson will referee Brentford's Premier League clash with Everton at Gtech Community Stadium. The Yorkshire official previously oversaw October's away game against Aston Villa, which the Bees drew 2-2 courtesy of goals from Yehor Yarmoliuk and Kristoffer Ajer. Including that meeting at Villa Park, Pawson has had the whistle for six fixtures this season, handing out 26 yellow cards and one red. Igor Thiago scored twice as Brentford were held to a 2-2 draw by Everton in a dramatic Premier League encounter at Gtech Community Stadium. The Bees twice took the lead through their in-form striker but were ultimately pegged back by a resilient Everton side, who struck late on to deny the hosts all three points. Thiago’s brace saw him reach 21 goals and become the club’s highest goalscorer in a single Premier League season. Beto and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall were on target for the Toffees. Vantage London

On that date, President Donald Trump signed the Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act, which permanently raises the debt limit for Subchapter V bankruptcies from $3,424,000 to $7.5 million. If you lend, lease, or sell to midsize companies, expect to see more Subchapter V cases. These bankruptcy cases are designed to move quickly, with the owners having more leverage than they would in a traditional Chapter 11. Subchapter V took effect in February 2020. Congress designed it for small businesses that could not afford the expense and delay of a traditional Chapter 11. Congress realized that Chapter 11 was not one-size-fits-all and that smaller companies needed a streamlined path of reorganization. At the start, a company qualified only if its debts totaled less than about $2.7 million. During the pandemic, Congress raised the cap to $7.5 million. That increase expired in June 2024, and the cap fell to roughly $3 million. Inflation adjustments pushed it to $3,424,000. The new law ends the rollercoaster ride. Congress passed it with little controversy. the House approved it by voice vote in September, and the Senate followed without amendment. The $7.5 million limit has no expiration date. It will adjust for inflation every three years, so expect it to creep upward. The higher limit applies only to cases filed on or after November 10, 2026. A company that filed on November 9 is measured against the old $3,424,000 cap. The debt limit cap is based on the company’s debts on the day it files for bankruptcy protection. Secured and unsecured debts count against the cap. Four rules decide who qualifies: Consider a contractor that owes its bank $4 million and its suppliers $1.5 million. The owner has also lent the company $2 million, and a customer has sued for $3 million in a case still pending. On paper, the company owes $10.5 million. For Subchapter V, only $5.5 million counts, and the contractor qualifies. Creditors can challenge a debtor’s eligibility, and the arithmetic deserves a careful look. We have previously written on the key differences between Subchapter V and traditional Chapter 11. Here is a refresher on the differences that affect creditors: Subchapter V is already popular. Debtors were already doing everything possible to get below the cap. With the limit doubled, inevitably debtors will file more Subchapter V cases. When they file, don’t tarry. Expect a faster timeline, no competing plan, and owners who may keep their equity. The 90-day plan deadline leaves little time to prepare. And remember that you have a potential ally in the Subchapter V trustee, whose job is facilitate an effective reorganization. In that role, the trustee acts as a negotiator, mediator, and information gatherer. content: As the calendar gets set to turn to December, it's time to crown a final fall champion. Beyond AI News Summaries: The Legal Challenges Raised by Like Company v. Google - IPWatchdog
content:
“Szpunar’s Opinion offers a valuable framework for generative AI and press publishers’ rights…[and] also reveals copyright’s limits.” The Opinion delivered by Advocate General Maciej Szpunar on November 3, 2026, in Like Company v. Google (C-250/25), the first generative artificial intelligence (AI) case to reach the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), is a significant development in the application of EU copyright law to generative AI. As IPWatchdog has already reported on the facts of the case, this article will explore its wider legal implications, including questions the Opinion addresses only briefly. One significant aspect of the Opinion concerns questions the Advocate General recommends the Court should not answer. Szpunar regards the questions about Gemini’s training as inadmissible, both because the evidence does not establish that the claimant’s publications were used for training and because training does not constitute an online use within Article 15 of Directive 2019/790 (the CDSM Directive), which protects press publishers against certain uses by information society service providers (paragraphs 45–57). The position may differ for copyright in the underlying journalistic works: authors’ reproduction rights are not subject to that same limitation. If the Court declines to answer the training questions, the Advocate General’s further discussion will remain persuasive analysis rather than a ruling on their merits. That discussion nevertheless raises a difficult territorial issue: can the commercial deployment in the EU of a model trained elsewhere bring earlier reproductions abroad within the reach of EU copyright law? Szpunar doubts that subsequent commercialization alone provides a sufficient connection (paragraphs 60–69). He also considers scraping from servers situated in the EU as a possible, albeit imperfect, connecting factor, and calls for legislative clarification (paragraphs 70–73). AI development disperses collection, storage, training and deployment across jurisdictions. The applicable law should therefore be assessed by identifying the allegedly infringing act and the exclusive right invoked, rather than treating the entire process as a single territorial event. Neither a broad effects-based approach nor exclusive reliance on server location offers a satisfactory answer. The Advocate General considers that reproductions made to train large language models may, in principle, qualify for the text-and-data-mining (TDM) exception in Article 4 of the CDSM Directive (paragraphs 99–109). That possibility depends on lawful access, the absence of an effective reservation of rights and compliance with the three-step test (paragraphs 110–152). The opt-out mechanism preserves scope for licensing; the commercial impact of AI training cannot, by itself, establish infringement where the legislature has authorized certain uses. More controversially, Szpunar goes further, suggesting that developers relying on the exception should demonstrate that they have taken measures (paragraphs 132–133). The concern is understandable, but it raises a question of legal architecture. Training reproductions and subsequent outputs are distinct acts. Article 4 does not expressly make the legality of training conditional on a particular design of generated responses. Output safeguards may be relevant to evaluating prejudice to rightholders under the three-step test, but their role should be explained without turning them into an additional, freestanding condition of the exception. The Opinion distinguishes training from retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which retrieves material to formulate answers to user requests. Szpunar considers that RAG may involve online uses within Article 15 (paragraphs 167–169), while the TDM exception does not cover operations undertaken for this different purpose (paragraph 179). Technical copies made during retrieval may nevertheless fall within the temporary-reproduction exception in Article 5(1) of Directive 2001/29 (the InfoSoc Directive). The Advocate General persuasively separates the commercial value of information retrieval from any independent economic significance of the temporary copies (paragraphs 180–184). Otherwise, the commercial character of a digital service could neutralize an exception intended to accommodate technical processes. The harder issue is lawful use: it depends on how the chatbot accesses the publication and what it subsequently produces. Circumventing effective restrictions may affect reliance on the exception, while an answer containing protected expression may constitute a separate restricted act (paragraphs 185–190). This becomes particularly difficult where publishers permit search indexing but object to AI-generated answers. The Advocate General observes that, in Google’s case, the same bots may serve indexing and AI functions, so blocking access through robots.txt may also affect search visibility (paragraph 228). If publishers cannot refuse one use without risking another, the practical exercise of their rights may depend on market structure. The European Commission’s investigation announced in December 2025 into Google’s use of online content for AI-related services illustrates why competition law may be relevant alongside copyright. That does not establish an antitrust infringement; it shows that exclusive rights alone may not resolve the problem. Perhaps the most consequential part of the Opinion concerns when an AI-generated answer reproduces a press publication. Szpunar favours ordinary reproduction principles over an AI-specific test, asking whether protected material has been copied and remains recognizable (paragraphs 193–196). The approach respects technological neutrality, but Article 15 establishes a related right for press publishers, distinct from authors’ originality-based protection. The exclusion of individual words and very short extracts also matters: communicating the same news does not necessarily reproduce protected subject matter. The Opinion’s example involving a report about dolphins illustrates the difficulty. Although an AI answer conveys much of the same information in different words and appears to share at least one sentence with the source (paragraph 204), the Advocate General considers infringement unlikely on the facts examined (paragraph 239). That conclusion should not be generalized into a rule that one matching sentence can never suffice. It instead exposes uncertainty about the boundary between protected reproduction and excluded very short extracts. There is a further paradox. A less accurate summary may be less likely to reproduce recognizable expression, even though invented details attributed to a publisher could cause reputational or other harm. Such harm is not necessarily addressed by the press publishers’ right in Article 15; other legal regimes may be relevant. The Opinion also gives weight to whether the answer substitutes for the original article, allowing users to dispense with consulting it (paragraph 202). Yet substitution and reproduction are not interchangeable. A chatbot may reproduce protected passages without replacing an entire article; conversely, a comprehensive factual summary may eliminate the incentive to visit the source without reproducing protected expression. The Court should clarify whether substitution is a legal requirement or merely evidence of the extent to which protected material has been appropriated. Copyright does not guarantee continued traffic to a publisher’s website. In a footnote, the Advocate General leaves open whether the exceptions for reporting current events and quotation in Article 5(3)(c) and (d) of the InfoSoc Directive might apply to chatbot answers (footnote 238). This is no peripheral issue: Article 15(3) of the CDSM Directive makes those exceptions applicable to press publishers’ rights. Even where an answer reproduces protected material, an exception may therefore matter. Quotation generally requires a relationship of engagement or “dialogue” with the quoted material, as discussed in Pelham (C-476/17) and Spiegel Online (C-516/17). An answer merely replacing an article may struggle to satisfy that rationale, although the assessment depends on its actual purpose and presentation. Reporting current events raises a different question. AI answers may identify sources and serve an informational purpose, but that alone cannot establish the exception: the use must satisfy its conditions, including the extent justified by the informatory purpose. Systematic repackaging of others’ reporting should not automatically be treated as protected news reporting. The Court would usefully clarify the distinction. Under Article 3(2) of the InfoSoc Directive, Szpunar suggests that a chatbot may make a press publication available where protected material is systematically recognizable in responses to related queries, to the point of substituting for the original (paragraphs 210–214). He seeks to distinguish isolated responses from a service that effectively provides access to protected publications. Yet generative systems can produce different answers to similar prompts, making systematic recognizability difficult to establish. The Advocate General appropriately distinguishes ordinary queries from artificial prompts designed to circumvent normal operation (footnote 221). A deeper issue remains: is systematic recognizability a substantive condition of the making-available right or an evidentiary consideration adapted to generative systems? The latter is preferable. Article 3(2) concerns access to protected subject matter at a place and time individually chosen by members of the public; it does not expressly demand repeated reproductions. Repeated recognizable outputs may provide strong evidence, but elevating repetition into a separate legal requirement risks narrowing an existing exclusive right. Attribution is crucial because Article 15 addresses uses by information society service providers, while excluding private or non-commercial uses by individual users. Drawing an analogy with YouTube and Cyando (Joined Cases C-682/18 and C-683/18), Szpunar considers whether a chatbot provider deliberately facilitates infringing acts, including through its business model or failure to take measures expected of a diligent operator (paragraphs 217–222). The analogy is useful but imperfect. Those cases concerned platforms facilitating access to user-uploaded material, whereas chatbots generate responses through systems designed and operated by their providers. Two distinctions matter. First, inadequate safeguards cannot themselves establish that protected material has been reproduced or made available: the existence of a restricted act must be assessed separately from responsibility for it. Second, the hosting exemption reflected in Article 6 of the Digital Services Act applies to information stored at a recipient’s request. Whether and to what extent it can apply to particular chatbot activities requires analysis; it should not simply be assumed to shield provider-generated answers. The relevant role of the provider, rather than the label “AI”, should guide the inquiry. Szpunar’s Opinion offers a valuable framework for generative AI and press publishers’ rights, rejecting both unlimited protection for publishers and automatic immunity for AI providers. Three issues particularly warrant clarification: whether economic substitution is a condition or merely evidence of reproduction; whether systematic recognizability is a substantive requirement of making available; and how the exceptions for quotation and current-events reporting apply to AI-generated answers. The Opinion also reveals copyright’s limits. Where publishers cannot effectively reject AI uses without sacrificing search visibility, competition law may have a role that an expansive reading of exclusive rights cannot properly perform.
